1.pericope_label: From whence come wars and fightings among you? ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have

schools.summary: Barnes prefers domestic broils and party strifes, traces the same spirit from a brawl in the street to the conquests of Alexander and Napoleon, and turns the comparison into an indictment of the illustrious conqueror; Ellicott quotes Bishop Moberly's figure of desires posted and picketed all over us like soldiers in the devil's army; Robertson distinguishes the chronic campaign from the separate battles and remarks that modern church disturbances are old enough in practice.

Gill canvasses national wars, theological disputes and oppressive lawsuits before settling on quarrels about honours and riches; Calvin denies the literal sense altogether, since the language is metaphorical and the military terms stand for lusts mustered in the heart, and holds that the soul indulging wicked lust is insatiable.

Clarke takes the wars literally, citing Josephus for the insurrections raised against the Romans and the factions that massacred each other, and notes that the Christians of the time had neither power nor political consequence enough to raise contentions; Wesley marks the members as the first seat of the war, whence proceeds the war of man with man, king with king, nation with nation.

Henry agrees the Jews were a seditious people whom the corrupt Christians addressed here had joined, draws the moral that what is sheltered under a pretence of zeal for God often comes from pride and revenge, and warns that when we speed not in prayer it is because we ask amiss.

debates.question: Does the second verse read ye kill or ye envy?

positions.view: ye kill; the substitution has no manuscript authority and was conjecture
ye envy; to kill does in no way suit the context
ye kill stands, but a full stop after it removes the difficulty
ye kill, understood of the heart, since he that hateth his brother is a murderer

outliers.claim: the partition of Poland by Austria, Prussia and Russia is a stain upon their justice and policy which no lapse of time can wash out

themes: From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?
Ye lust, and have not: ye kill, and desire to have, and cannot obtain: ye fight and war, yet ye have not, because ye ask not.

3.pericope_label: Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss: the friendship of the world is enmity with God

schools.summary: Barnes observes that men who go to war pray, and that the covetous keep a form of worship while asking success in engagements founded on covetousness, so that unanswered prayer proves the motive wrong rather than the promise false; Ellicott says the received reading of the address is wrong and only the feminine should stand, and denies any middle ground between God and the world; Robertson agrees the masculine is spurious and Syrian, and thinks the literal sense of the charge more in harmony with the preceding verses.

Gill reads the address figuratively, of those who set their affections on the world instead of God, and reports versions that omit the feminine; Calvin says they wished to make God the minister of their own lusts, recalls that Pliny ridiculed men who so abuse the ears of God, and insists that those who take the words literally do not sufficiently observe the context.

Clarke glosses the phrase as asking evilly, calls the idiom Jewish, and reports a suggestion that the prayer meant was for the conversion of the heathen, on whose failure the petitioners thought it lawful to extirpate them; he leans to the figurative reading of the address but allows that perhaps something more than spiritual adultery is intended, and ends that when the world gets into the church, the church becomes a painted sepulchre; Wesley reads it of those who have broken faith with their rightful spouse.

debates.question: Is the charge of adultery literal or figurative?

positions.view: figurative, of a covenant with God broken by love of the world
probably literal, and so may take in more than Christians
figurative, but perhaps something more is intended

outliers.claim: renunciation of the world is the earliest severance from it, not a forsaking of it when tired and clogged with its delights

themes: Ye ask, and receive not, because ye ask amiss, that ye may consume it upon your lusts.
Ye adulterers and adulteresses, know ye not that the friendship of the world is enmity with God? whosoever therefore will be a friend of the world is the enemy of God.

5.pericope_label: The spirit that dwelleth in us lusteth to envy: but he giveth more grace

schools.summary: Barnes reports that few passages have given expositors more perplexity, rejects the escapes offered, and concludes the writer condensed into his own words a truth taught everywhere rather than citing a particular place; he also refuses to make the spirit the Holy Spirit, since the Greek will not well bear it. Ellicott is unbothered by the missing text, since the substance sufficed without a slavish adherence to the form, and offers the jealous sense of the Spirit regarding us as his own; Robertson finds no passage precisely like it, floats the possibility that the citation points forward to the proverb quoted next, and says there is no way to decide positively.

Calvin cuts the knot by referring the citation to what has already been said, that the friendship of the world is adverse to God, and reads the clause as a question arguing from the contrary, since envy proves malignity while the Spirit proves himself bountiful; Gill records only that some have looked in the New Testament and some in an apocryphal book.

Clarke calls the verse exceedingly obscure, lists four candidate texts, and observes that there is not a critic in Europe who has considered the passage and not been puzzled by it; he reads the sense contrary to the received translation, since the Spirit dwelling in a genuine Christian excites strong desires against envy.

positions.view: man's own spirit, our disposition as we are by nature
the Holy Spirit, and the sense is the opposite of the received rendering
the Holy Spirit, yearning after us jealously in a good sense

outliers.claim: he prints his paraphrase while refusing to claim it is right, since no critic in Europe has escaped being puzzled by the verse

themes: Do ye think that the scripture saith in vain, The spirit that dwelleth in us lusteth to envy?
But he giveth more grace. Wherefore he saith, God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.

7.pericope_label: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you

schools.summary: Robertson counts ten aorist imperatives in the four verses and hears urgency in each, glossing the first two as military terms; Ellicott calls submission the hardest advice of all to a man reliant on himself and then finds the one place where pride may be a stimulant for good, quotes the Shepherd of Hermas that the devil can fight but cannot conquer, and takes the verse as proof of the personality of Satan; Barnes prefers direct resistance to argument, since none who yield are safe and none who refuse are unsafe, and takes the hands for the instruments by which we execute what the heart devises.

Calvin explains the connecting particle from the bounty of the Spirit, requires humility rather than obedience in general, raises against himself the objection that daily experience refutes the promise that Satan flees, and answers that fleeing means being routed, since however often he returns he departs vanquished; he also distinguishes the salutary sorrow that leads to repentance from the mourning denounced as a curse. Gill applies the submission to worldly things and lists the acknowledgments of unworthiness that Abraham, Job and the publican made.

Clarke notes the delicacy of the expression that when a soul sets out to seek God, God sets out to meet it, divides cleansing and sanctification between the hands and the heart, thinks the address to sinners begins a new appeal that should have started a new verse, and doubts such charges of dissolute living could have been addressed to a church few in number, without wealth, and persecuted.

debates.question: Does the devil in fact flee from those who resist him?

positions.view: the promise seems refuted by experience, so fleeing must mean being routed and returning vanquished
he flees beaten and ashamed; he can fight but cannot conquer
resistance is safe because no one who yields in the least is safe

outliers.claim: the vocabulary of laughter and pleasure shows a dissolute life is meant, which he doubts could describe a small, poor and persecuted Christian body

themes: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.
Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you. Cleanse your hands, ye sinners; and purify your hearts, ye double minded.
Be afflicted, and mourn, and weep: let your laughter be turned to mourning, and your joy to heaviness.
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.

11.pericope_label: Speak not evil one of another, brethren: there is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy

schools.summary: Barnes takes the law for the law of Christ and reads the whole against the quarrel over the binding force of the Mosaic ceremonies, drawing from it the principle that no laws bind the conscience but those Christ ordained; Ellicott defines the fault as setting up our own tribunals, in which we are at once prosecutor, witness, law, lawgiver and judge, and quotes Bengel that it is not our part to judge since we cannot carry out our sentence; Robertson condemns the tone of superiority to law and notes the emphatic pronoun in the closing question.

Calvin finds beneath the fault a disease innate in human nature, that every one would have all others live according to his own fancy, and holds that so much is taken from the law as a man claims of authority over his brethren; Gill lists the forms slander takes and applies the title of lawgiver to the Father and to the Son alike.

Clarke reports the rabbinic maxim that no one speaks evil of his brother without denying God, traces detraction to the devil's calumny in Eden, and dissents from the majority reading, holding that the law meant is the Jewish law and the lawgiver God Almighty, since he finds but few references to Christ or his gospel in the epistle; Wesley answers the closing question with a poor, dying worm.

Henry takes the verb to cover anything that may hurt another, so that evil things must not be spoken even when true unless there is necessary occasion, and reads the offence against the law as censuring a brother over things the law has left indifferent.

debates.question: What law is judged, and who is the one lawgiver?

positions.view: the law of Christ, and the lawgiver is Christ, the legislator of the church
the Jewish law, and the lawgiver is God Almighty as the Jews acknowledged him
the title belongs to the Father and to the Son alike

outliers.claim: from the closest examination of the epistle he finds but few references to Jesus Christ or his gospel, the writer keeping his Jewish creed and maxims constantly in view

themes: Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law: but if thou judge the law, thou art not a doer of the law, but a judge.
There is one lawgiver, who is able to save and to destroy: who art thou that judgest another?

13.pericope_label: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city: ye know not what shall be on the morrow

schools.summary: Barnes calls the opening a phrase designed to arrest notice, quotes a description of the eastern trader who repeats his circuit for years until he can return home prosperous, gathers the classical writers on the uncertainty of the future, and presses that no solid hope can be built on a mist; Ellicott sharpens the figure so that the vapour is not merely life but the men themselves and all belonging to them; Robertson finds the merchant in the verb and adds the touch that the speaker would be pointing at the city on a map.

Calvin insists that the form of speaking is not what is reproved but the arrogance of mind behind it, since the servants of God everywhere speak unconditionally of the future, and locates the fault in men who claimed a whole year while having no moment in their own power; Gill puts it plainly, that no man can secure a day, an hour, or a moment.

Clarke matches the opening to the Hebrew word for come, describes the Jewish traffic carried on camels from Tyre to Rome, tells the rabbinic story of the man warned by the angel of death that he would die within thirty days, and sets Pliny, the son of Sirach and Homer's generations of leaves side by side, asking which borrowed from which.

debates.question: Is it the life or the man that is called a vapour?

positions.view: the life, on which no solid hope can be built
the men themselves and all belonging to them, which is the sharper thrust

outliers.claim: no scruple ought to be entertained as though it were a sin to omit the qualifying clause, since Scripture's holy servants speak unconditionally of future things

themes: Go to now, ye that say, To day or to morrow we will go into such a city, and continue there a year, and buy and sell, and get gain:
Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.

15.pericope_label: For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that

schools.summary: Barnes denies that the words must always be said in so many words, since that might become a mere ostentatious form offensive by constant unmeaning repetition, locates the boasting in reliance on one's own skill and sagacity, and quotes Cotton Mather's principle that the ability to do good imposes an obligation to do it; Ellicott presses the tense of the condition, if the Lord have willed it, distinguishes the doctrine from fatalism in even its best form, and identifies the boasting with the pride of life rather than the innocent gladness of living; Robertson calls the formula the proper attitude of mind and not a charm to be uttered always in words, and notes the word for vaunting is common in Aristophanes.

Calvin finds a twofold condition, if we live and if the Lord will, and specifies that the will meant is God's governing counsel rather than the will expressed in the law; he holds that more than a passing speech is condemned, since their minds were inebriated with vanity so as to disregard God, and answers the contemptuous reply that such warnings tell men only what they know by charging that they sinned through contempt and not ignorance. Gill extends the closing maxim to all the good the epistle has urged.

Clarke brings two illustrations, the rabbinic bridegroom who answered the bystanders that he would do it whether the Lord willed or not and died that night, and the man in Lucian killed by a falling tile while promising to come to supper; he hears in the boasting men exulting that they are free of superstition and can live independently of God, and quotes an old English book on those who thank God for their unholiness.

debates.question: Must the qualifying clause actually be spoken?

positions.view: no; saying it always would become an ostentatious and unmeaning form
the practice deserves careful attention, though omitting it is no sin
the words themselves are what ought to be said in place of the boast

outliers.claim: a heathen satirist's joke about a man killed by a falling tile should shame the Christian who presumes on tomorrow

themes: For that ye ought to say, If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.
But now ye rejoice in your boastings: all such rejoicing is evil.
Therefore to him that knoweth to do good, and doeth it not, to him it is sin.
